jsonld.name: Calorie Calculator
jsonld.description: Free calorie calculator: maintenance calories (Mifflin-St Jeor), daily targets to lose or gain weight, a week-by-week projection to your goal weight with dates, macros and safety checks.

mainEntity.name: How accurate is this calorie estimate?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is a predictive estimate, not a direct measurement of energy expenditure. Individual metabolism and activity vary, so use it as a starting point and compare it with your real-world trend over several weeks.

mainEntity.name: Why does activity level matter so much?

acceptedAnswer.text: Activity level changes the estimate because everyday movement and exercise contribute to total energy expenditure. The size of that difference varies substantially between people.

mainEntity.name: Why am I not losing weight at my calculated deficit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common causes include underestimating portion sizes, overestimating exercise calories burned, or a maintenance calorie level that's actually different from the formula's estimate — tracking actual results over a few weeks helps calibrate.

mainEntity.name: Is it safe to eat below my calculated deficit?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single calorie floor that is appropriate for every adult. Very-low-calorie diets can create nutritional and other health risks and should only be undertaken with appropriate clinical supervision.

mainEntity.name: Should I recalculate my calorie needs as I lose weight?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — as body weight changes, so does your BMR and total calorie needs, so recalculating every few weeks during an active weight loss or gain phase keeps your target accurate.

mainEntity.name: Is a 500-calorie deficit always the right target?

acceptedAnswer.text: A fixed 500-calorie deficit is not appropriate for everyone. The size of a deficit should be individualized rather than treated as a guaranteed weekly weight-loss formula.

mainEntity.name: Why does my projected weight loss slow down over time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because energy needs can change as body weight, body composition and activity change. The projection is a simplified model and should be compared with real-world trends rather than treated as a guaranteed forecast.

mainEntity.name: What is a calorie calculator and what does it tell me?

acceptedAnswer.text: A calorie calculator estimates how many calories you burn in a day (maintenance calories) from your sex, age, height, weight and activity level. It then adjusts that number up or down for your weight goal, so you get a daily calorie target.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate a calorie deficit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Subtract your target intake from your maintenance calories. For a man with maintenance of 2,396 calories who eats 1,896, the deficit is 500 calories a day. At about 7,700 calories per kilogram, that is roughly 0.45 kg (1 lb) a week.

mainEntity.name: How many calories should I cut to lose weight?

acceptedAnswer.text: A common range is 250 to 750 calories a day below maintenance, which is about 0.2 to 0.7 kg (0.5 to 1.5 lb) a week. A larger cut needs a doctor or dietitian's advice, and your target should not fall under the minimum your health professional recommends.

mainEntity.name: What is a calorie surplus and how big should it be?

acceptedAnswer.text: A calorie surplus is eating more than your maintenance calories. For gradual weight gain, 250 to 500 calories a day above maintenance is typical. Adding 300 calories suggests about 0.27 kg (0.6 lb) a week.

Net calories are calories eaten minus calories burned through exercise. If you eat 2,000 and burn 350 exercising, your net is 1,650. This calculator builds exercise into the activity factor, so do not subtract workouts again.

mainEntity.name: Which activity level should I choose?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pick the lowest level that honestly fits your week: 1.2 for little or no exercise, 1.375 for 1–3 workouts, 1.55 for 3–5, 1.725 for 6–7 and 1.9 for a physical job plus training. If unsure, choose lower and adjust after two to three weeks.

mainEntity.name: Why does another calorie calculator give me a different number?

acceptedAnswer.text: Calculators use different equations. This one uses Mifflin-St Jeor. Others use the 1919 Harris-Benedict equation or equations from the Institute of Medicine. For the example man the maintenance figure is 2,396 with Mifflin-St Jeor and 2,504 with Harris-Benedict, about 100 calories apart.

mainEntity.name: How many calories do men and women need a day?

acceptedAnswer.text: The US Dietary Guidelines give roughly 1,600 to 2,400 calories for adult women and 2,000 to 3,000 for adult men, depending on age and activity. Use the calculator for a figure based on your own height and weight.
Many dietitians treat 1,200 for women and 1,500 for men as a floor not to pass without medical supervision. Below that it is harder to get enough nutrients, so talk to a doctor or dietitian first.

mainEntity.name: Can I use this calculator to count the calories in my food?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. It sets a daily target. To count food calories, log what you eat in a food diary or use nutrition labels, then compare your average intake with the target.
